notes.section: Part 16 — The PM and Business Lens
notes.text:
The full causal chain is: workload → resource pressure → bottleneck → optimization → metric change → business consequence.
Example 1: long context → larger KV cache → more memory pressure → lower concurrency → higher cost per request.
Example 2: better continuous batching → higher GPU utilization → more tokens per GPU-hour → lower cost per token.
Example 3: quantization → smaller weights → less memory traffic → faster inference → lower serving cost, with a possible quality trade-off.
This is the level to aim for: not memorizing vocabulary, but explaining why a technical change matters economically.

notes.doc_title: Podcast — Why LLM Inference Is Really a Memory Problem
notes.section: Part 4 — What is the KV Cache?
notes.text:
When an LLM generates the next token, it needs information about previous tokens. Attention has already computed Key and Value states for those prior tokens. Instead of recomputing them every step, the system stores them in a KV cache.
So KV cache is a classic trade-off: use more memory to avoid repeated compute.
In one sentence: use more GPU memory in exchange for less repeated computation.
But KV cache grows as context length grows. More simultaneous users also mean more active KV caches. So: longer context + higher concurrency = more GPU memory pressure.

notes.doc_title: Podcast — Why LLM Inference Is Really a Memory Problem
notes.section: Part 14 — AI Infrastructure Is Mostly Trade-offs
notes.text:
Every optimization solves one problem and often creates another.
KV cache: less compute, but more memory. Batching: better throughput, but possibly worse latency. Tensor parallelism: more compute capacity, but more communication. Quantization: lower memory and cost, but possibly lower quality.
The important PM mental model is: there is no free optimization.
The job is not ‘make everything faster.’ The job is: for this workload, which bottleneck matters most, and which trade-off are we willing to make?

notes.section: PART 11 — WHY THIS MATTERS FOR BROADCOM
notes.text:
Broadcom can benefit from custom ASIC growth in two ways.
First, it can help hyperscalers build the accelerator itself.
Second, it can also supply networking and connectivity around those accelerators.
That means Broadcom may benefit from both compute growth and networking growth.
This is also what makes Broadcom special.
It does not necessarily earn money only from ASICs; it may also earn money from infrastructure such as SerDes, Ethernet, switching, and optical connectivity.

Today we are going to connect several concepts that often appear together in AI infrastructure discussions: ASICs, hyperscalers, Broadcom, SerDes, and NVLink.
In this episode we connect several AI infrastructure concepts that often appear together: ASIC, hyperscaler, Broadcom, SerDes, and NVLink.
The goal is not just to memorize definitions. The goal is to understand the system: who designs what, why hyperscalers build custom chips, how Broadcom participates, and why networking is becoming almost as important as compute.
The point is not to memorize definitions but to understand the whole system: who is responsible for what, why big companies build their own chips, where Broadcom participates, and why network interconnect is becoming more and more important.

A useful way to think about Broadcom is:
The hyperscaler defines what the chip needs to do.
Broadcom helps turn those requirements into scalable, manufacturable silicon.
The simplest way to understand it:
The hyperscaler decides “what chip do I want.”
Broadcom helps it solve “how to actually turn that into a high-performance chip that can be mass-produced.”
The hyperscaler usually owns:
- the AI model and workload
- performance targets
- latency targets
- power targets
- software and compiler stack
- product roadmap
- deployment strategy
Broadcom contributes more heavily in:
- silicon implementation
- high-speed I/O
- SerDes
- networking IP
- chip interfaces
- physical design
- packaging integration
- process-node integration
- manufacturability
The hyperscaler is more the “demand side + product owner + workload expert.”
Broadcom is more the “semiconductor engineering + connectivity + implementation partner.”
